sections.guidingQuestion: Which molecule directly uses a DNA template to synthesize a transcript?
sections.explanation:
RNA polymerase binds a DNA region and uses one DNA strand as the template to synthesize an RNA strand. As it advances, a local part of the duplex unwinds, incoming ribonucleotides pair with exposed DNA bases and the RNA nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds. The DNA strands re-form the duplex behind the enzyme; unlike replication, the product is RNA rather than double-stranded DNA.

For a given gene, promoter orientation determines which DNA strand is transcribed. Do not call one physical chromosome strand the template for every gene: the two strands can each serve as the template for different genes, with orientation set by promoters.

Transcription copies a selected DNA region into one RNA transcript. RNA polymerase reads a DNA template and creates phosphodiester links in the nascent RNA; after it passes, the local DNA duplex reforms. This is not a second round of DNA replication.

RNA polymerase locally exposes a template strand and links ribonucleotides into a transcript using complementary base pairing. As the enzyme moves, the parental DNA strands rejoin; the DNA sequence is not consumed or permanently changed by routine transcription. RNA transcription copies a selected region rather than producing a second chromosome, so a cell can transcribe a gene repeatedly between divisions. The amount of transcript produced depends on initiation frequency, while the amount of protein subsequently made also depends on translation and RNA and protein turnover.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which 5′→3′ RNA sequence is transcribed from template 3′-TAC-5′?
sections.explanation:
During RNA synthesis, DNA A pairs with RNA U, DNA T pairs with RNA A, and DNA C and G pair with RNA G and C respectively. Hydrogen bonding supports the matching of a ribonucleotide to its template base while RNA polymerase creates the covalent sugar–phosphate backbone of the new RNA.

The RNA sequence is complementary and antiparallel to the template DNA strand. It matches the coding DNA strand apart from U in RNA in place of T in DNA, provided both sequences are written 5′ to 3′. Confusing these two DNA strands reverses expected RNA and codon answers.

Check the polarity of all three aligned molecules: coding DNA 5′-ATG GCT TAA-3′, template DNA 3′-TAC CGA ATT-5′, and mRNA 5′-AUG GCU UAA-3′. RNA is complementary to the template and matches the coding sequence apart from U replacing T.

If the DNA template reads 3′-TAC CGA ATT-5′, the RNA transcript reads 5′-AUG GCU UAA-3′. The corresponding coding DNA strand is 5′-ATG GCT TAA-3′, which matches the RNA apart from thymine being replaced by uracil. Hydrogen bonding selects each matching ribonucleotide, but covalent phosphodiester bonds join the RNA strand. A question that merely gives a DNA sequence without indicating template versus coding strand and direction cannot have one uniquely specified RNA answer.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why can a non-dividing neuron repeatedly transcribe one gene?
sections.explanation:
A DNA gene can be transcribed repeatedly because RNA polymerase reads the sequence without consuming nucleotides from the DNA template or converting DNA into RNA. The double helix re-forms when the temporary transcription bubble passes, preserving the base order.

A neuron may remain active for years with little or no cell division while making fresh RNA copies from the same DNA genes. Maintenance and DNA repair matter because a persistent template mutation could alter all later transcripts produced from that gene.

DNA is read without being consumed. Long-lived nondividing neurons can therefore transcribe the same gene repeatedly throughout their life; transcription alone does not change the inherited template. DNA damage is still possible, so stable does not mean chemically indestructible.

A differentiated neuron may need the same protein for years without duplicating its entire genome. RNA polymerase temporarily separates a short stretch of DNA, constructs an RNA transcript, and leaves the DNA bases in their original order; the DNA duplex can re-form immediately behind it. Multiple transcripts can be synthesized from a gene at different times. Replication, by contrast, produces another DNA molecule before division. This difference explains why ongoing gene expression is compatible with maintaining a stable inherited DNA sequence in cells that rarely divide.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which is a major stage at which a cell regulates whether a gene is expressed?
sections.explanation:
Most cells share a large collection of genes, but they do not transcribe every gene at the same time. Transcription is an early control point for gene expression: if a gene is not transcribed, little or no new mRNA from it becomes available for translation.

A liver cell and a pancreatic beta cell can carry the same insulin gene while producing different quantities of its transcript. Regulatory proteins and DNA regions are further explored in HL gene expression, but the essential idea is selective transcription rather than a change to DNA sequence.

Not every gene is transcribed continuously. Regulatory choices at transcription help cells with essentially the same genome maintain different patterns of protein synthesis and different specialized functions. Gene expression describes molecular activity, not a change in the DNA genotype.

A cell may contain a gene in its genome while producing little or none of that gene's RNA. Regulatory signals can change transcription initiation at its promoter, changing the number of transcripts available for translation. Different amounts of a polypeptide can change metabolic activity or cellular structure and thus alter phenotype. This helps explain why cells derived from one zygote develop different functions despite inheriting very similar DNA sequences. Presence of a gene therefore does not imply that it is continuously expressed in every cell type.

sections.guidingQuestion: What is the direct product of translating an mRNA coding region?
sections.explanation:
Translation converts the sequence of mRNA codons into an amino-acid sequence, rather than copying a nucleic acid strand. Ribosomes assemble amino acids through peptide bonds in the order specified by the mRNA. A resulting polypeptide may fold and undergo additional processing before functioning as a protein.

The codon AUG at the beginning of a coding sequence specifies methionine and usually signals translation initiation. Stop codons terminate the coded chain instead of specifying an extra amino acid. The final polypeptide is read from the amino terminus toward the carboxyl terminus.

Translation links the information in mRNA codons to the order of amino acids in a polypeptide. A ribosome does not translate genomic DNA, nor does it manufacture amino acids from codons: charged tRNA molecules deliver the amino acids that the ribosome joins by peptide bonds.

Ribosomes read a messenger RNA in successive three-base codons. Suitable amino-acid-bearing tRNAs pair their anticodons with the exposed codons, and the ribosome joins the delivered amino acids with peptide bonds. The direct product is a polypeptide chain, which may require folding or further modification to become a functional protein. Translation neither makes another RNA strand nor alters the parental DNA sequence. A start codon establishes a reading frame, whereas a stop codon signals termination and does not add another amino acid.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which molecule carries an amino acid to the translating ribosome?
sections.explanation:
mRNA supplies the readable codon sequence; the small ribosomal subunit binds the mRNA; tRNAs carry particular amino acids into the assembled ribosome. Two tRNAs can occupy the ribosome simultaneously while one amino acid is transferred to the growing polypeptide chain.

Ribosomes contain rRNA and proteins and catalyse peptide-bond formation. A tRNA anticodon recognizes a matching mRNA codon; tRNA is not itself the inherited DNA template. The components cooperate in translation but have different molecular jobs.

mRNA supplies the code; small and large ribosomal subunits organize decoding and peptide-bond formation; tRNAs match codons while delivering bound amino acids. The large subunit holds two relevant tRNAs simultaneously during elongation, where the chain can be transferred.

Three distinct molecules cooperate in translation. The mRNA is the sequence being read, tRNAs are adaptor molecules bearing amino acids and complementary anticodons, and the ribosome positions them so amino acids can be linked by peptide bonds. Each mRNA codon is a group of three nucleotide bases read 5′ to 3′. A complementary tRNA anticodon pairs antiparallel to that codon, helping the ribosome select a tRNA loaded with the corresponding amino acid.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why is a triplet code necessary to encode 20 standard amino acids?
sections.explanation:
Four RNA bases yield 4² = 16 possible doublets, insufficient for 20 standard amino acids, whereas 4³ = 64 triplets provide enough codons. Codons are read without overlap in the established reading frame; many different codons can specify one amino acid.

Degeneracy means more than one codon can specify a particular amino acid, making some changes silent. The standard genetic code is nearly universal across life, providing strong evidence of shared ancestry; specialized genetic codes such as some mitochondrial codes are known exceptions.

Four possible bases yield 4² = 16 doublets, too few for 20 standard amino acids, but 4³ = 64 triplets. Degeneracy means different triplets can code for the same amino acid. The code is nearly universal; exceptions in some organisms and organelles should not be denied.

A triplet assembled from four different RNA bases has 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 possible combinations. These include codons for 20 standard amino acids and stop signals, so more than one codon can specify the same amino acid: the code is degenerate. Each codon, however, normally has only one meaning in the standard code; it does not randomly specify different amino acids on successive readings. Triplets are read consecutively from the established reading frame, making an insertion of one base far more disruptive than a synonymous substitution.

sections.guidingQuestion: How far does a ribosome normally advance along mRNA after adding one amino acid?
sections.explanation:
In elongation, an aminoacyl-tRNA enters the A site in response to the next codon. The growing chain, attached to the tRNA in the P site, is transferred by peptide-bond formation to the amino acid in the A site. The ribosome then translocates three bases along the mRNA, enabling the process to repeat.

The chain is elongated at its carboxyl end, with peptide bonds joining successive amino acids. Translocation preserves the codon reading frame; a shift by a single base would change all later codon groupings.

During elongation, an aminoacyl-tRNA matches the next codon, a peptide bond forms, and the ribosome advances by three bases along 5′→3′ mRNA. The chain grows through successive peptide transfers; the ribosome does not add RNA nucleotides during this step.

The next matching aminoacyl-tRNA binds the ribosomal A site; a peptide bond forms so the growing chain is transferred to that tRNA. Translocation moves the ribosome one codon in the 5′→3′ direction, shifting tRNAs through the P site towards exit. This is a conceptual step sequence, not a time-resolved observation.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which change can produce a different amino acid in a polypeptide?
sections.explanation:
A DNA point mutation may change an mRNA codon and thus replace an amino acid. The biochemical properties of the replacement can affect folding, stability or activity, but not every substitution produces a change in the encoded polypeptide.

In sickle-cell disease, a substitution in the beta-globin gene can replace glutamate with valine in beta-globin, affecting hemoglobin properties. The example shows that a molecular sequence difference can have consequences at cell and organism levels, not that all variants cause disease.

A point substitution can alter one codon and thereby change one amino acid. Altered side-chain chemistry may affect folding, binding or an active site; the effect depends on protein context. The sickle-cell HBB substitution is one example, but a substitution is not always harmful.

A DNA base substitution can result in a changed mRNA codon and a different amino acid in the translated chain. Depending on its location and properties, that replacement may alter protein folding or function, but some substitutions are synonymous and do not change the amino-acid sequence. A premature stop signal can shorten the product and often has more severe effects. Work through the DNA-to-mRNA-to-polypeptide sequence before predicting phenotype. Not every DNA mutation affects a protein, and even a changed amino acid is not necessarily biologically damaging.

sections.guidingQuestion: In which direction is a newly synthesized RNA chain extended?
sections.explanation:
RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA by extending a 3′ end, so the RNA grows 5′→3′ while the template DNA is read 3′→5′. Translation reads mRNA from its 5′ end toward its 3′ end. These are two distinct kinds of directional processes.

The ribosome then reads the mature mRNA 5′→3′ and adds amino acids to the carboxyl end of a growing polypeptide. These orientations are different aspects of a directional mechanism, not optional arrow placements on a diagram. sections.guidingQuestion: What is the principal role of a promoter?
sections.explanation:
A promoter is a regulatory DNA sequence near a gene that helps position the transcription machinery. In eukaryotes, transcription factors can bind promoter sequences and assist RNA polymerase recruitment; promoter orientation helps select the DNA template.

Not every three-base DNA sequence is a transcription start. Cell-specific regulation can increase or decrease initiation, allowing one gene's transcription to change without changing its base sequence.

A promoter is a DNA sequence that helps recruit and position the transcription machinery near the start of a gene. Promoter orientation determines which strand is the template. Transcription factors can bind promoter DNA, but named factors are not required in this HL understanding.

A promoter is DNA, not a molecule made by RNA polymerase. Its sequence and position help determine where transcription begins and which strand is used as a template. In eukaryotic cells, transcription factors assemble at regulatory DNA and recruit or enable the polymerase; the guide does not require memorizing individual factor names. A promoter cannot guarantee that every copy of a gene is transcribed continuously. Different cell types and conditions alter the availability of the machinery, thereby changing the rate of RNA production.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which is a clear example of a gene whose final product is not a polypeptide?
sections.explanation:
Large regions of eukaryotic DNA are non-coding. Some DNA regions control when genes are expressed, introns are removed from pre-mRNA, telomeres protect chromosome ends, and genes for rRNA or tRNA yield functional RNAs rather than polypeptides.

Some non-coding sequences are regulatory, structural or transcribed into functional RNA. Others have no established function. Avoid the incorrect extremes that all non-coding DNA is useless or that all DNA is protein coding.

Noncoding DNA can be functional. Required eukaryotic examples include regulatory DNA, introns, telomeres, and genes whose final products are tRNA or rRNA. Distinguish DNA that is transcribed into functional RNA from DNA segments that regulate another transcription event.

A DNA segment may affect gene expression without specifying a polypeptide sequence. Promoters and enhancers are regulatory sequences, while introns can be included in a primary eukaryotic transcript and removed before translation. Some genes produce functional RNA molecules that are never translated into proteins. Therefore 'non-coding' should not be equated with 'useless'. When predicting a protein from DNA, identify the coding sequence and the mature mRNA reading frame rather than treating every nucleotide in the genome as an amino-acid instruction.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which process removes introns from eukaryotic pre-mRNA?
sections.explanation:
A typical eukaryotic protein-coding transcript is initially pre-mRNA containing introns and exons. Splicing removes introns and joins exons. A 5′ cap and 3′ poly-A tail help stabilize and process the RNA and contribute to efficient translation after export.

The order of retained exons establishes the final coding information. A poly-A tail is added enzymatically after RNA cleavage and is not simply a long DNA-encoded thymine tract copied verbatim. Pre-mRNA processing generally occurs in the nucleus.

Eukaryotic pre-mRNA maturation includes addition of a 5′ cap, a 3′ poly(A) tail, and removal of introns while exons are spliced together. The tail consists of RNA adenosine residues; it is not a poly-alanine protein. Processing supports RNA stability and proper use.

Eukaryotic protein-coding pre-mRNA undergoes intron removal, exon splicing, 5′ capping and 3′ polyadenylation before mature mRNA is typically exported for translation. Processing modifies the RNA transcript, not the DNA base sequence. Alternative exon combinations are discussed separately under D1.2.16.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which ribosomal site accepts the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA during elongation?
sections.explanation:
In a typical eukaryotic process, the small ribosomal subunit and initiation factors associate with the 5′ end of mRNA and scan toward an AUG start codon. The initiator tRNA pairs with the start codon, and the large ribosomal subunit joins to form the functional ribosome.

The initiation tRNA occupies the P site. During subsequent elongation, an incoming aminoacyl-tRNA occupies the A site, the growing chain is transferred from P to A, and a deacylated tRNA exits through E after translocation. Two tRNAs can be bound simultaneously.

At initiation, the small ribosomal subunit engages mRNA near its 5′ end and finds the start codon; initiator tRNA and large subunit assemble a functional ribosome. During elongation, the A site receives an incoming charged tRNA, P holds the peptidyl-tRNA, and E releases empty tRNA.

During eukaryotic translation initiation, the small ribosomal subunit associates with the mRNA and helps identify a start codon, ordinarily AUG. The initiator tRNA recognizes that codon and establishes the reading frame; the large ribosomal subunit joins to form a working ribosome. Only then can repeated elongation cycles add further amino acids. Initiation specifies where the codon sequence starts to be interpreted, while elongation builds the chain. Do not confuse the AUG start codon with a stop codon, which signals termination rather than an amino acid.

sections.guidingQuestion: What is removed when proinsulin is converted to mature insulin?
sections.explanation:
A new polypeptide is not always the final functional molecule. Folding, cleavage, covalent modification, subunit association or export can be essential to activity. The resulting product should not be described as necessarily functional the instant translation ends.

Human preproinsulin is targeted into the endoplasmic reticulum where a signal peptide is removed, yielding proinsulin. Proinsulin folds and forms disulfide bonds; in secretory granules proteolytic removal of its connecting C-peptide generates mature insulin A and B chains linked by disulfide bonds.

Preproinsulin enters the secretory pathway and loses its signal peptide, becoming proinsulin. Removal of connecting C-peptide produces mature insulin, with A and B chains stabilized by disulfide bonds. Translation alone does not immediately generate the functional secreted hormone.

Translation creates an amino-acid chain but does not guarantee that the new product already has its final shape and function. A polypeptide may fold, associate with other chains or undergo specific cleavage. In the insulin example, proinsulin is processed by removing a connecting peptide, producing mature insulin with appropriately linked chains. Such events are post-translational changes; they differ from removing introns from pre-mRNA before translation. The Guide does not require memorizing every possible protein modification to understand this distinction.

sections.guidingQuestion: What type of macromolecule is principally degraded by a proteasome?
sections.explanation:
Cells continually replace damaged, misfolded or unneeded proteins. The proteasome is a cellular proteolytic complex that breaks targeted proteins into short peptides; subsequent cellular peptidases can yield amino acids for reuse.

A functional proteome depends on the balance between transcription, translation, protein processing and removal. Protein breakdown does not mean that an entire gene is deleted from DNA; the cell can synthesize a new copy of the protein later.

An actively maintained proteome requires removal of damaged or no-longer-needed proteins as well as new synthesis. Proteasomes degrade many intracellular proteins into shorter fragments, and cellular peptidases recover reusable amino acids. Not all proteins are destroyed exclusively by proteasomes.

A cell does not regulate protein abundance only by changing how much mRNA it makes. Once synthesized, proteins have different lifetimes and some become damaged or unnecessary. Proteasomes break selected polypeptides into smaller peptides that can be further degraded to reusable amino acids. Recycling saves materials and prevents accumulation of malfunctioning components. If synthesis remains constant but degradation accelerates, steady-state protein amount generally decreases. This post-translational control is distinct from the RNA breakdown that regulates how long a message remains available to ribosomes.

questions.prompt: Use a labelled sequence or appropriate molecular example to explain the ribosome advances one codon at a time. Identify and correct this claim: "The ribosome moves one nucleotide after each added amino acid."
questions.answer: In elongation, an aminoacyl-tRNA enters the A site in response to the next codon. The growing chain, attached to the tRNA in the P site, is transferred by peptide-bond formation to the amino acid in the A site. The ribosome then translocates three bases along the mRNA, enabling the process to repeat. The chain is elongated at its carboxyl end, with peptide bonds joining successive amino acids. Translocation preserves the codon reading frame; a shift by a single base would change all later codon groupings. It advances by one three-base codon per elongation cycle.
markingPoints: During elongation, an aminoacyl-tRNA matches the next codon, a peptide bond forms, and the ribosome advances by three bases along 5′→3′ mRNA
The chain grows through successive peptide transfers; the ribosome does not add RNA nucleotides during this step
Correct the common inference: It advances by one three-base codon per elongation cycle.

questions.prompt: Which change can produce a different amino acid in a polypeptide?

options.feedback: Correct. A DNA point mutation may change an mRNA codon and thus replace an amino acid.
Consider why “Any synonymous substitution” does not answer this question. Degenerate codons can preserve an amino acid, while some substitutions change structure or function.

questions.prompt: Use a labelled sequence or appropriate molecular example to explain sequence changes can alter a protein. Identify and correct this claim: "Every single-base substitution must change the polypeptide sequence."
questions.answer: A DNA point mutation may change an mRNA codon and thus replace an amino acid. The biochemical properties of the replacement can affect folding, stability or activity, but not every substitution produces a change in the encoded polypeptide. In sickle-cell disease, a substitution in the beta-globin gene can replace glutamate with valine in beta-globin, affecting hemoglobin properties. The example shows that a molecular sequence difference can have consequences at cell and organism levels, not that all variants cause disease. Degenerate codons can preserve an amino acid, while some substitutions change structure or function.
markingPoints: A point substitution can alter one codon and thereby change one amino acid
Altered side-chain chemistry may affect folding, binding or an active site; the effect depends on protein context
Correct the common inference: Degenerate codons can preserve an amino acid, while some substitutions change structure or function.

options.feedback: Correct. RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA by extending a 3′ end, so the RNA grows 5′→3′ while the template DNA is read 3′→5′.
Consider why “3′→5′” does not answer this question. It reads template DNA 3′→5′ and synthesizes RNA 5′→3′.
Consider why “Both directions alternately” does not answer this question. It reads template DNA 3′→5′ and synthesizes RNA 5′→3′.

questions.prompt: Use a labelled sequence or appropriate molecular example to explain directions in transcription and translation. Identify and correct this claim: "RNA polymerase reads coding DNA 5′→3′ to make matching mRNA."
questions.answer: RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA by extending a 3′ end, so the RNA grows 5′→3′ while the template DNA is read 3′→5′. Translation reads mRNA from its 5′ end toward its 3′ end. These are two distinct kinds of directional processes. A gene's coding strand has the mRNA-like sequence 5′→3′, but polymerase reads the opposite template strand. The ribosome does not move 3′→5′ merely because its tRNAs have complementary antiparallel anticodons. It reads template DNA 3′→5′ and synthesizes RNA 5′→3′.
markingPoints: Distinguish the directions of two different processes: RNA synthesis extends 5′→3′ while DNA template reading is 3′→5′; the ribosome moves along mRNA 5′→3′ while the polypeptide grows from N-terminus to C-terminus
5′ and 3′ labels belong to nucleic acids, not peptides
Correct the common inference: It reads template DNA 3′→5′ and synthesizes RNA 5′→3′.

questions.prompt: What is the principal role of a promoter?

options.feedback: Correct. A promoter is a regulatory DNA sequence near a gene that helps position the transcription machinery.
Consider why “Encode an anticodon” does not answer this question. Promoters are DNA control regions for transcription initiation.

questions.prompt: Use a labelled sequence or appropriate molecular example to explain promoters determine where transcription begins. Identify and correct this claim: "A promoter is the amino-acid site where the ribosome adds methionine."
questions.answer: A promoter is a regulatory DNA sequence near a gene that helps position the transcription machinery. In eukaryotes, transcription factors can bind promoter sequences and assist RNA polymerase recruitment; promoter orientation helps select the DNA template. Not every three-base DNA sequence is a transcription start. Cell-specific regulation can increase or decrease initiation, allowing one gene's transcription to change without changing its base sequence. Promoters are DNA control regions for transcription initiation.
markingPoints: A promoter is a DNA sequence that helps recruit and position the transcription machinery near the start of a gene
Promoter orientation determines which strand is the template
Correct the common inference: Promoters are DNA control regions for transcription initiation.

questions.prompt: Use a labelled sequence or appropriate molecular example to explain not every dna sequence encodes a protein. Identify and correct this claim: "Any DNA sequence not translated must be biologically useless."
questions.answer: Large regions of eukaryotic DNA are non-coding. Some DNA regions control when genes are expressed, introns are removed from pre-mRNA, telomeres protect chromosome ends, and genes for rRNA or tRNA yield functional RNAs rather than polypeptides. Some non-coding sequences are regulatory, structural or transcribed into functional RNA. Others have no established function. Avoid the incorrect extremes that all non-coding DNA is useless or that all DNA is protein coding. Regulators, introns, telomeres and functional RNA genes are non-protein-coding.
markingPoints: Noncoding DNA can be functional
Required eukaryotic examples include regulatory DNA, introns, telomeres, and genes whose final products are tRNA or rRNA
Correct the common inference: Regulators, introns, telomeres and functional RNA genes are non-protein-coding.

questions.prompt: Which process removes introns from eukaryotic pre-mRNA?

options.feedback: Correct. A typical eukaryotic protein-coding transcript is initially pre-mRNA containing introns and exons.
Consider why “DNA helicase separation” does not answer this question. Introns are removed from pre-mRNA; retained exons make up mature mRNA.
Consider why “Protein glycosylation” does not answer this question. Introns are removed from pre-mRNA; retained exons make up mature mRNA.
Consider why “Ribosomal peptide elongation” does not answer this question. Introns are removed from pre-mRNA; retained exons make up mature mRNA.

questions.prompt: Use a labelled sequence or appropriate molecular example to explain eukaryotic transcripts are processed. Identify and correct this claim: "Introns are translated into the final protein before they are removed."
questions.answer: A typical eukaryotic protein-coding transcript is initially pre-mRNA containing introns and exons. Splicing removes introns and joins exons. A 5′ cap and 3′ poly-A tail help stabilize and process the RNA and contribute to efficient translation after export. The order of retained exons establishes the final coding information. A poly-A tail is added enzymatically after RNA cleavage and is not simply a long DNA-encoded thymine tract copied verbatim. Pre-mRNA processing generally occurs in the nucleus. Introns are removed from pre-mRNA; retained exons make up mature mRNA.
markingPoints: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA maturation includes addition of a 5′ cap, a 3′ poly(A) tail, and removal of introns while exons are spliced together
The tail consists of RNA adenosine residues; it is not a poly-alanine protein
Correct the common inference: Introns are removed from pre-mRNA; retained exons make up mature mRNA.

questions.prompt: Use a labelled sequence or appropriate molecular example to explain alternative splicing changes exon combinations. Identify and correct this claim: "Alternative splicing permanently deletes unused exons from chromosome DNA."
questions.answer: One eukaryotic gene can produce several mature mRNA versions if different combinations of exons are joined during processing. These transcripts may then be translated into related but distinct polypeptide isoforms with differing domains or functions. Alternative splicing does not require an immediate mutation in the DNA sequence. Instead, the cell regulates which portions of the primary RNA transcript remain in the finished mRNA. It helps expand proteomic diversity without proportionally increasing the number of protein-coding genes. It alters RNA processing, not the inherited DNA sequence.
markingPoints: Alternative splicing produces different exon combinations from transcripts of one DNA gene
Multiple mature RNAs can therefore lead to different polypeptide isoforms without changing the original nucleotide sequence
Correct the common inference: It alters RNA processing, not the inherited DNA sequence.

Consider why “E site” does not answer this question. Incoming aminoacyl-tRNAs generally use A; P holds the growing chain and E allows exit.

questions.prompt: Use a labelled sequence or appropriate molecular example to explain assemble the initiation complex. Identify and correct this claim: "All incoming aminoacyl-tRNAs bind first to the E site."
questions.answer: In a typical eukaryotic process, the small ribosomal subunit and initiation factors associate with the 5′ end of mRNA and scan toward an AUG start codon. The initiator tRNA pairs with the start codon, and the large ribosomal subunit joins to form the functional ribosome. The initiation tRNA occupies the P site. During subsequent elongation, an incoming aminoacyl-tRNA occupies the A site, the growing chain is transferred from P to A, and a deacylated tRNA exits through E after translocation. Two tRNAs can be bound simultaneously. Incoming aminoacyl-tRNAs generally use A; P holds the growing chain and E allows exit.
markingPoints: At initiation, the small ribosomal subunit engages mRNA near its 5′ end and finds the start codon; initiator tRNA and large subunit assemble a functional ribosome
During elongation, the A site receives an incoming charged tRNA, P holds the peptidyl-tRNA, and E releases empty tRNA
Correct the common inference: Incoming aminoacyl-tRNAs generally use A; P holds the growing chain and E allows exit.

questions.prompt: Use a labelled sequence or appropriate molecular example to explain functional proteins may require processing. Identify and correct this claim: "The ribosome directly translates free mature two-chain insulin as its initial product."
questions.answer: A new polypeptide is not always the final functional molecule. Folding, cleavage, covalent modification, subunit association or export can be essential to activity. The resulting product should not be described as necessarily functional the instant translation ends. Human preproinsulin is targeted into the endoplasmic reticulum where a signal peptide is removed, yielding proinsulin. Proinsulin folds and forms disulfide bonds; in secretory granules proteolytic removal of its connecting C-peptide generates mature insulin A and B chains linked by disulfide bonds. Translation first makes a precursor, which is enzymatically processed to mature insulin.
markingPoints: Preproinsulin enters the secretory pathway and loses its signal peptide, becoming proinsulin
Removal of connecting C-peptide produces mature insulin, with A and B chains stabilized by disulfide bonds
Correct the common inference: Translation first makes a precursor, which is enzymatically processed to mature insulin.

questions.prompt: Use a labelled sequence or appropriate molecular example to explain proteasomes recycle cellular protein building blocks. Identify and correct this claim: "Proteasomes convert DNA directly into amino acids."
questions.answer: Cells continually replace damaged, misfolded or unneeded proteins. The proteasome is a cellular proteolytic complex that breaks targeted proteins into short peptides; subsequent cellular peptidases can yield amino acids for reuse. A functional proteome depends on the balance between transcription, translation, protein processing and removal. Protein breakdown does not mean that an entire gene is deleted from DNA; the cell can synthesize a new copy of the protein later. They degrade proteins, contributing amino acids to cellular recycling.
markingPoints: An actively maintained proteome requires removal of damaged or no-longer-needed proteins as well as new synthesis
Proteasomes degrade many intracellular proteins into shorter fragments, and cellular peptidases recover reusable amino acids
Correct the common inference: They degrade proteins, contributing amino acids to cellular recycling.
